note: Recent PRISMA review of AI in clinical risk management, covering incident reporting, falls and medication error.
title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming patient safety with intelligent systems: A systematic review
explain_beginner: The question, pulling together everything published up through early 2024, does AI actually make hospital care safer in practice, across things like medication mistakes, falls, bedsores, and general risk management, or mostly just in early stage testing. Safety officers and hospital administrators cared because they needed an up to date picture spanning many types of harm at once, since most individual AI safety studies only look at one narrow problem, and interest in this area had grown sharply after 2019. Reviewing 52 studies pulled from an initial 662 candidates, the authors found genuinely strong results in specific narrow tasks, for example one combined decision support system correctly flagged roughly three out of four risky drug prescriptions before they were filled, and separate machine learning models predicted patient falls and pressure injuries with very high statistical accuracy in the data used to build them. What it does not settle is whether any of this translates into hospitals that are measurably safer once these tools are actually running day to day, since very few of the described systems had received formal regulatory clearance or had been tested for real world impact outside the original study.
explain_business: A hospital safety committee scanning the AI market for patient safety tools can use this review's specific numbers, such as 74 percent precision on prescription interception or 0.92 to 0.94 AUC on pressure injury prediction, as a rough benchmark for what good looks like when comparing vendor claims in these categories. Because the review found most of these tools lack formal regulatory clearance and limited real world validation, a health system adopting one is often taking on a device that has cleared a research bar rather than a regulatory or deployment bar, and should plan for its own real world testing period before scaling use widely. Budgeting should account for workflow integration and staff training, since the review names user acceptance and integration into existing systems as recurring, unresolved barriers rather than solved problems vendors can simply hand over. The absence of formal FDA or EU MDR clearance for many of these tool categories at the time of the review means procurement teams need to check current regulatory status themselves, deal by deal, rather than assume the category is broadly cleared. This is most relevant during vendor shortlisting for the four use cases the review covers, adverse event detection, medication error interception, fall prediction, and pressure injury prediction.
explain_practitioner: Method, a systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidance, searching three major databases in February 2024 and screening with the Rayyan tool, yielding 662 initial records narrowed to 52 included studies spanning 2007 to 2024 with a clear increase in publication volume after 2019. Specific results, a hybrid clinical decision support system reached 74 percent precision intercepting problematic drug orders, fall prediction models reported accuracy figures as high as 98 to 99.7 percent, and pressure injury prediction using random forest models achieved AUCs of 0.92 to 0.94, while natural language processing tools were noted as effective at pulling safety relevant signal out of unstructured clinical notes for adverse event detection. These numbers are generally reported against either no prior automated tool or against simpler rule based alerting, rather than head to head against another AI system. The authors state clear limitations, despite these strong lab metrics, few of the systems reviewed had achieved FDA or EU Medical Device Regulation approval, real world validation remained limited relative to the promising retrospective results, evaluation metrics were inconsistent across studies making comparison difficult, and user acceptance and workflow integration barriers persisted as unresolved practical issues.
